The key distinction for the test is that with「～ていただけませんか」, the listener performs the action, whereas with the causative auxiliary「～(さ)せていただけませんか」, the speaker is the one who performs it.

The second clause must then express the speaker’s will, duty, command, or strong judgment, often with ～べきだ, ～つもりだ, or ～なければならない. The pattern 「～といっても」acknowledges that the preceding statement is true, while indicating that the reality in the following clause is not as extensive or impressive as the listener might assume.
default.q.test-1-q23-23.explanation: The pattern 「～といっても」 follows the plain form of a verb, adjective, or noun (with nouns and na-adjectives, it may be used directly without だ). It is used when the speaker wants to correct or clarify that reality does not reach the level the listener might associate with the preceding statement. Its overall meaning is “although I say..., in reality only...” or “even though it is called..., it is merely...,” often narrowing or modestly qualifying a claim. For example: 「料理ができるといっても、卵焼きが作れるくらいです。」 (Although I can cook, I can only make something like rolled omelets.) To avoid confusing it with choice (d), 「～にしては」, remember that 「といっても」 prevents exaggerating the degree of the statement just made, whereas 「にしては」 means “for...” or “considering...” and comments on something that is unexpectedly different from the normal standard for that subject.

default.q.test-1-q23-23.why.1: ✓ (b) 「～といっても」 means “although one says...” or “even though it is said that...”. It acknowledges the statement in the first clause, while the following clause adds information showing that reality is not as extreme as one might imagine.

The pattern means "leave ... out," "put ... aside," or "let's stop ...", expressing a request to set unnecessary matters aside and proceed with the main task. For example:「冗談は抜きにして、まじめに話し合いましょう。」(Let's stop joking and discuss this seriously.) To remember it, connect it with the original meaning of the kanji「抜」(to pull out, remove), which helps distinguish it from patterns expressing cause or contrast that do not involve removing an object.

The grammar ～限り（は） expresses a core condition: as long as the state in the first clause continues, the event in the second clause also continues.
default.q.test-1-q25-25.explanation: The pattern 「～限り（は）」usually combines with the plain form of a verb or adjective, or with a noun followed by である, to establish a prerequisite condition that continues over time. It means "as long as..." or "so long as...", with the nuance that the following state or commitment remains unchanged while the preceding condition continues. A typical example is 「日本にいる限り、日本語を使わざるを得ない。」, meaning "As long as I am in Japan, I have no choice but to use Japanese." To distinguish it from other options, focus on the kanji 「限」(limit): 「～限り（は）」sets a time or state boundary, unlike 「～によっては／～次第では」, which means that the result varies depending on the person or circumstances.

default.q.test-1-q25-25.why.2: ✓ (c) The pattern ～限り（は） accurately expresses a prerequisite condition meaning “as long as …” or “provided that …,” with the following state continuing.
default.q.test-1-q25-25.why.3: ✗ (d) The meaning “it will probably be around...,” expressing an estimated time, does not match the grammatical function of ～限り（は）.

The pattern 「たとえ～ても」expresses a concessive assumption, emphasizing that even if a hypothetical situation occurs, the following result or decision will not change.

It is used to emphasize that even if a difficult or extreme hypothetical condition occurs, the intention, action, or result in the following clause remains unchanged. For example: たとえ両親に反対されても、私は夢を諦めません (Even if my parents oppose me, I will not give up on my dream). To identify this pattern quickly, remember the correlative pair「たとえ...ても/でも」, which signals a hypothetical concessive construction, and avoid confusing it with structures expressing a standpoint, such as「～として」, or the superlative preference pattern「～に限る」.

It emphasizes a proportional, progressive change: the more the action or state in the first clause increases, the more strongly the result in the second clause develops. A typical example is: 「外国語は使えば使うほど上手になります」(The more you use a foreign language, the more proficient you become.) In multiple-choice questions, the conditional 「～ば」may sometimes be omitted, leaving only the dictionary form with 「～ほど」, as in 使えば使うほど becoming 使うほど. The progressive meaning remains, which helps distinguish this pattern from expressions of limitation or ordinary advice.

It emphasizes a prerequisite that must be fulfilled. The pattern means: "Unless A is done, B cannot be performed or occur." Compare: 「実際に食べてみないことには、おいしいかどうか分かりません。」(Unless you actually try eating it, you cannot know whether it is delicious.) A quick test-taking clue is the negative form in both clauses, which immediately rules out choices expressing a reason, asking permission, or presenting a special case.

The pattern 「～てからでないと／～てからでなければ」emphasizes a prerequisite: unless the action in the preceding clause has been completed, the action or state in the following clause cannot occur or progress.
default.q.test-1-q9-9.explanation: This pattern combines with the te-form of a verb (V-てからでないと / V-てからでなければ) and emphasizes that the first action is a necessary prerequisite that must be completed first. The second clause always has a negative or impossible meaning, often with endings such as ～できない (cannot), ～わけにはいかない (cannot or must not), or ～無理だ (impossible). Thus, the pattern means: "unless... / if ... has not been done, ... cannot be done." For example:「上司に相談してからでないと、この件は決定できません。」(Unless I consult my supervisor first, I cannot decide this matter.) Unlike ordinary「V-てから」, which simply expresses sequence and can be followed by an affirmative sentence,「～てからでないと」must be followed by a negative expression of difficulty or impossibility.

It strongly reflects the speaker's subjective feelings and often occurs with degree adverbs such as 「よく」, 「本当に」, 「ずいぶん」, and 「なんと」. To distinguish this use from other meanings of 「～ものだ」, such as general principles or past habits, remember that the exclamatory use focuses on an intense spontaneous feeling at the time of speaking. It can also combine with 「～たいものだ」to express a strong wish. Example: 「日本に来てもう5年が経ったのか、時間が経つのは本当に早いものだ。」 (Has it really been five years since I came to Japan? Time passes so quickly.)

It expresses a firm resolve or definite statement that an action or mistake will never happen again. The complete meaning is “not do something a second time” or “never do it again,” often used after a bad experience when the speaker feels regret or warns themselves to learn from it. For example, 「あんなまずい店には二度と行くものか。」means “I will never go to such a terrible restaurant again.” To distinguish it from other choices, note that the kanji 「二度」(nido—two times) combines with the negative 「ない」to create the emphatic message “there will be no second time,” rather than expressing a cause or conjecture.

The structure「～ものか／～もんか」strongly and decisively denies something, reflecting the speaker’s emotion or firm determination. It means “absolutely not” or “as if I would ….”
default.q.test-10-q11-11.explanation: In essence, the grammar pattern 「～ものか／～もんか」 (with the polite forms 「～ものですか／～もんですか」) combines with the plain form: the dictionary form of a verb (V-る), an i-adjective (A-い), a na-adjective retaining な (Na-な), or a noun followed by な (N-な). It uses the form of a rhetorical question to challenge someone or express one's own thoughts, conveying strong rejection and complete negation. It means "absolutely not," "never," or "How could I possibly...?" For example, to show determination never to return to a terrible restaurant, one can say: 「あんなまずい店、二度と行くものか。」 (There is no way I would ever go to such a terrible restaurant again!). To avoid confusion on the test, remember that the final 「か」 makes it a rhetorical question used for negation. This is completely different from 「～ものだ」 (used for exclamation or an obvious truth) and 「～ものだから」 (used to explain a cause or make an excuse).

The core meaning of the grammar pattern ～たら is to express a hypothetical condition in the future or a point in time followed by the next action.
default.q.test-10-q12-12.explanation: The pattern ～たら is formed by changing a verb, i-adjective, or noun into the short past form (た-form) and adding ら (V-たら, A-かったら, Na/N-だったら). It is used to present a hypothetical situation that has not yet occurred or to establish a temporal sequence between two events. In a complete sentence, it can be translated as “If [event A occurs], then [action B will occur]” or “After [A is completed], [do B].” For example: 「仕事が終わったら、一緒に飲みに行きましょう。」(After work is finished, let’s go out for a drink together.) The key distinction from easily confused conditional patterns such as ～と (which cannot be followed by volitional expressions) and ～ば (which restricts invitations and commands) is that ～たら is highly conversational, and the following clause can freely take endings expressing desire, requests, or invitations, such as ～たい, ～てください, and ～ましょう.

default.q.test-10-q12-12.why.1: ✓ (b) ～たら is a basic conditional pattern expressing “if …, then …” or a sequence of events meaning “after …, then ….”

It has a formal, objective tone and covers a broad subject area, so it often appears in speeches, scientific reports, conferences, and news. It indicates that an action or piece of information concerns the topic stated before に関して. For example: 「環境問題に関して、専門家による議論が行われた。」 (“A discussion by experts was held concerning environmental issues.”). Distinguish 「に関して」(about; concerning) from 「において」(in; at, referring to a place or context), and note that 「に関して」is more formal than the familiar 「について」.

Because it predicts trouble, the following clause must describe an unwanted negative event and cannot express intention, a command, or a beneficial result. The sentence means: “If you dare to object to what that person says, there will definitely be serious trouble.” Another example is: 「授業中に居眠りをしようものなら、先生にひどく怒られる。」(If you were to fall asleep in class, the teacher would be furious.) Do not confuse this with 「V-potential + ものなら」, which expresses a strong but difficult-to-realize wish. Remember that the clause after 「V-ようものなら」must describe a bad outcome, allowing you to eliminate positive or intentional options quickly.

default.q.test-30-q14-14.why.1: ✗ (b) 「～てごらん」 expresses advice or an invitation to try doing something, so it is unsuitable for stating a warning about a consequence.
default.q.test-30-q14-14.why.2: ✗ (c) Incorrect because 「勝つ」(to win) is a positive result, conflicting with the rule that the second clause of this pattern must always describe a bad outcome.
default.q.test-30-q14-14.why.3: ✓ (d) This is correct because 「大変なことになる」(something serious will happen) accurately expresses the unintended serious consequence characteristic of the pattern.

default.q.test-30-q15-15.explanation: The grammar pattern 「V-ない＋かぎり」 means "unless A is done / if A is not done, then...". It emphasizes a prerequisite, and the following clause must express a definite negative result, a negative judgment, or something that cannot be done. The complete sentence means: "Unless you climb mountains 3,000 meters or higher, you will not be able to see this flower." A quick test-taking tip: when you see 「～ないかぎり」 in the first clause, immediately look for definite negative endings such as 「～ない / ～できない」, while avoiding a seemingly affirmative expression disguised as a double negative, such as 「～なくもない」 in choice c. Reference example: 「パスポートを提示しないかぎり、入国することはできません。」(Unless you present your passport, you will not be allowed to enter the country.)

default.q.test-30-q15-15.why.3: ✗ (d) The idiom 「見るに見かねる」 means “unable to stand by and watch” a distressing situation, so it is completely inappropriate in the context of viewing flowers.

The grammar pattern 「〜に反して」 describes a result that is completely contrary to the initial expectation, so the following clause must express that it hardly rained.
default.q.test-30-q16-16.explanation: The pattern 「N + に反して」combines directly with nouns expressing thoughts, expectations, or predictions, such as 期待, 予想, and 予測. It indicates that the actual situation or result is completely contrary to the original expectation. The following clause must state an objective fact that occurred; conjectural forms such as だろう and かもしれない, as well as volitional or wishful expressions, cannot be used. The complete sentence means: "Contrary to the expectation that it would finally rain, in reality hardly a drop fell." Choice (c) may be tempting because it also expresses negation, but the conjectural ending 「だろう」does not fit this pattern. Compare: 「大方の予想に反して、新製品は大ヒットとなった。」(Contrary to most people’s predictions, the new product became a huge hit.)

default.q.test-30-q16-16.why.3: ✗ (d) The description of heavy rain causing floods that wash away houses shows the severity of the disaster; it does not express a result contrary to the expectation of rain.

It is used when the speaker postpones consideration of A in order to focus on the more urgent or important matter B. The completed sentence means: "Whether you go to university or not can be decided later, but at the very least, you have to take the exam first." For comparison:「値段はともかく、この料理はとても美味しい。」(Leaving the price aside, this dish is really delicious.) In this pattern, the clause after「〜はともかく」does not directly affirm or deny the matter set aside in the first clause, so eliminate b and d. The pattern 「～ながら（も）」 expresses a contradiction between awareness and reality, so the following clause must describe an action or state contrary to what is known, such as “cannot quit.”

The complete sentence means: "Although I know that cigarettes do nothing good for my health, I still cannot manage to quit." Compare: 「体に悪いと分かっていながら、夜遅くに甘いものを食べてしまう。」(Although I know it is bad for my health, I still end up eating sweets late at night.) Note that the second clause after 「～ながら」does not normally express volition, a command, or a natural continuation based on logic. Therefore, determined choices such as (a) 「やめようと決意した」should be eliminated.

The grammar pattern「〜にかかわらず」means “regardless of” or “irrespective of.” Therefore, the following clause must express a rule or command that applies regardless of personal feelings or preferences.
default.q.test-30-q19-19.explanation: The pattern 「N / V-る・V-ない ＋ にかかわらず」means "regardless of / irrespective of...". It describes a rule, action, or objective fact that is not affected by the condition in the first part, often involving paired opposites such as 好き嫌い, 男女, or 有無. The complete sentence means: "Once the food has been served, eat it all, whether you like it or not!" A typical example is 「このマラソン大会は、雨天にかかわらず予定通り開催されます。」(This marathon will be held as scheduled regardless of whether it rains.) For test-taking, remember that the second part usually expresses a principle, requirement, or equality, so it does not combine with permissive expressions such as 「〜てもいい」.
default.q.test-30-q19-19.why.0: ✗ (a) The past form 「おいしかった」expresses a subjective feeling and directly contradicts 「きらい」(dislike) in the preceding clause.
default.q.test-30-q19-19.why.1: ✗ (b) The expression allowing something unnecessary to be omitted, 「残してもいい」, is illogical when paired with the premise “regardless of whether one likes or dislikes the dish that has been served.”
default.q.test-30-q19-19.why.2: ✗ (c) The meaning “it is okay not to eat it” makes the sentence illogical and unnatural when referring to food one personally likes.
default.q.test-30-q19-19.why.3: ✓ (d) The imperative 「全部食べなさい」fits the meaning perfectly: once the food has been served, it must all be eaten whether one likes it or not.

After the contrastive conjunction「ものの」(although... but...), the following clause must express lingering feelings and an inability to decisively give up the intention of attending university.
default.q.test-30-q2-2.explanation: The key grammar pattern is 「V(ます) + きる / きれない」. The negative form 「～きれない」 expresses being unable to do something completely, carry it through to the end, or make a clean break, and often combines with emotional or psychological verbs such as あきらめる or 忘れる to express lingering regret or attachment. In this context, the complete sentence means: “Although I once gave up on going to university, I still cannot truly give up.” Compare: 「長年の夢だったので、一度の失敗ではあきらめきれない。」 (“Because it was a dream of many years, I cannot give up after just one failure”). The contrastive conjunction 「ものの」 is the key: since the first clause says “I gave up,” the second clause must express the opposite meaning, “I have not been able to give it up completely.” This immediately rules out 「あきらめざるをえない」 (“have no choice but to give up”), which has the same direction, and 「あきらめかねない」 (“may end up giving up”), which predicts an objective negative possibility.
default.q.test-30-q2-2.why.0: ✗ (a) The volitional form「 あきらめよう」(“let’s give up” / “will give up”) is semantically illogical after the contrastive conjunction「ものの」.
default.q.test-30-q2-2.why.1: ✗ (b) The pattern 「～かねない」 (“may; be at risk of”) predicts an objective negative consequence; it is not used for one’s own troubled feelings.
default.q.test-30-q2-2.why.2: ✗ (c) The pattern 「～ざるをえない」(to have no choice but to..., be forced to...) gives both clauses a sense of giving up, eliminating the contrast expressed by 「ものの」.
default.q.test-30-q2-2.why.3: ✓ (d) The negative potential pattern 「～きれない」(unable to completely do something) forms 「あきらめきれない」, correctly expressing the feeling of being unable to give up studying.

✅ Correct answer: (d) 決めかねる
The structure 「V-ます + かねる」expresses difficulty or inability to perform an action because of one’s position or circumstances. It fits the context of being unable to decide something concerning both people alone.
default.q.test-30-q20-20.explanation: The key N2 grammar pattern「V-ます (without ます) + かねる」is formal and polite, and is used to refuse or indirectly express that one "finds it difficult to" or "cannot" do something because of a psychological, positional, or professional concern. In the question, the completed sentence means: "Since this is a matter between the two spouses, it would be difficult for me to decide on my own." Learners often confuse the negative meaning of「〜かねる」(cannot do) with「〜かねない」, which positively indicates a risk ("could very well" or "there is a possibility that something bad will happen"). Another example:「個人情報に関するご質問には、お答えしかねます。」(We are unable to answer questions concerning personal information.)
default.q.test-30-q20-20.why.0: ✗ (a) 「〜しかない」 means “there is no choice but to...” or “must...”; this contradicts the sentence’s logic because one spouse cannot decide alone about a matter concerning both of them.
default.q.test-30-q20-20.why.1: ✗ (b) 「〜かねない」 means “may possibly/could result in something bad,” so its meaning and tone do not fit here.
default.q.test-30-q20-20.why.2: ✗ (c) 「〜ずにいられない」 means being unable to suppress one’s feelings and having to do something; it does not fit a context of being compelled by shared responsibility.
default.q.test-30-q20-20.why.3: ✓ (d) 「〜かねる」 means “find it difficult to” or “be unable to” due to one’s position or circumstances, precisely expressing the intended meaning of the sentence.

The pattern 「N＋を抜きにしては」means "without N" or "if N were absent" and requires a negative expression of impossibility in the following clause. Therefore, 「できなかっただろう」is the only correct choice.
default.q.test-30-q21-21.explanation: The grammar pattern 「N ＋ を抜きにしては」(or 「〜を抜きにして」) means "without N" or "if N is excluded." It emphasizes the special importance of N and states that the situation in the following clause would be impossible without it. The clause that follows normally expresses negation or impossibility, often with できない, 無理だ, あり得ない, or 成り立たない. The complete sentence means: "Without your cooperation, this work surely could not have been completed." For example: スタッフの努力を抜きにしては、このイベントの成功はあり得なかった。(Without the staff's efforts, the success of this event would have been impossible.) When you see 「〜を抜きにしては」, immediately look for a negative ending expressing impossibility in the following clause. This helps eliminate choices expressing an unavoidable obligation, such as 〜ざるを得ない, or hypothetical regret, such as 〜のに.
default.q.test-30-q21-21.why.0: ✗ (a) 「やらざるをえなかった」expresses unwillingness—“had no choice but to do it”—and does not fit a pattern requiring a negated possibility.
default.q.test-30-q21-21.why.1: ✓ (b) 「できなかっただろう」 means “surely would not have been able to do it,” perfectly matching the negative impossibility required after 「〜を抜きにしては」.
default.q.test-30-q21-21.why.2: ✗ (c) 「できなくもなかった」means “it was not that it was impossible” (implicitly affirming that it was possible), which contradicts the required negative meaning.
default.q.test-30-q21-21.why.3: ✗ (d) 「できただろうに」expresses regret that something “could have been done,” and is not used to assert a decisive prerequisite condition.

「～にしては」expresses a reality that differs from the usual standard or expectation. Therefore, describing someone nearly 30 years old as childlike (子どもっぽい) is completely appropriate.
default.q.test-30-q22-22.explanation: The pattern 「～にしては」combines with the plain form of a verb, adjective, or noun. With nouns and na-adjectives, だ is omitted. It means "despite..." or "considering...", and is used when the actual result differs significantly from the usual standard, expectation, or stereotype suggested by the preceding phrase. The complete sentence means: "Even though she is about to turn 30, she is still childish." The key distinction is the mildly critical suffix 「～っぽい」, which describes behavior or qualities that do not suit someone's age, such as an adult seeming childlike. This contrasts with 「～らしい」, which can praise someone for being typical or suitably mature. For comparison: 彼は日本に５年住んでいるにしては、日本語があまり上手ではない。(Despite having lived in Japan for five years, he is not very good at Japanese.)
default.q.test-30-q22-22.why.0: ✗ (a) 「大人らしい」 means “adult-like,” which is natural for someone aged 30. This conflicts with the contrastive meaning of 「～にしては」.
default.q.test-30-q22-22.why.1: ✗ (b) 「４０歳くらいにみえる」is merely an observation that someone looks older, and does not express the mismatch or atypical evaluation relative to their age required by the context.
default.q.test-30-q22-22.why.2: ✓ (c) 「子どもっぽい」(childish) accurately reflects the complete contrast with the maturity expected of someone approaching 30.
default.q.test-30-q22-22.why.3: ✗ (d) 「結婚しようと思った」 only expresses a personal intention in the past; it does not express a characteristic or contrasting evaluation related to the time reference.

The pattern 「〜ないこともない」 means “it is not that … is impossible.” It expresses reluctant agreement or a tentative possibility, fitting the premise 「条件次第では」 (depending on the conditions).
default.q.test-30-q24-24.explanation: The structure 「V-ないこともない」uses the negative form of a verb to create a double negative meaning “it is not that I cannot...” It expresses a possibility or reluctant acceptance in a cautious, modest way, often with a condition. The complete sentence means: “I have been quite busy lately, but depending on the circumstances, it is not that I cannot accept the job.” Example: 「給料を上げてくれるなら、残業しないこともない。」 (If you raise my salary, it is not that I cannot work overtime.) When a hypothetical clause such as 「〜次第では」 (“depending on...”) opens the possibility of doing something, choose 「〜ないこともない」 rather than 「〜わけにはいかない」, which expresses inability due to moral obligations or responsibilities.

The grammar pattern 「〜からといって」 (“just because...”) is often followed by a negative or prohibitive clause such as 「〜てはいけない」, expressing that one cannot overdo something merely for that reason.
default.q.test-30-q3-3.explanation: The pattern「V/A/N (plain form) + からといって」means "just because..." or "even if one says that...". It warns that the reason in the first clause cannot be used to justify arbitrary action or an absolute judgment. Therefore, the following clause must generally contain a negative or prohibitive form, such as 〜わけではない, 〜とは限らない, or 〜てはいけない. The complete translation is: "Even if you have finished your exams, you must not spend all day just fooling around like that." Example:「日本人だからといって、誰もが敬語を正しく使えるわけではない。」(Just because someone is Japanese does not mean that everyone can use honorific language correctly.) For the N2 exam, when「〜からといって」appears in the first clause, quickly eliminate choices expressing simple affirmation, permission, or positivity, and focus on negative or admonitory endings.

The pattern 「〜どころか」 means “far from...” or “not only does it not..., but instead...”. Therefore, the following clause must express the complete opposite of “decrease,” making 「ふえる一方だ」 (“keep increasing”) the best choice.

Combined with「V-る + 一方だ」(continue increasingly in one direction), it describes a continuous change contrary to the initial expectation. The complete sentence means: "Although many laws have been enacted, the number of cases has not decreased at all; instead, it continues to increase." Compare「風邪は治るどころか、悪化する一方だ。」(Far from getting better, the cold is steadily getting worse.) When you see「A どころか」, look for a following clause that reverses A completely and eliminate choices moving in the same direction, such as (a).

Do not confuse it with the intransitive verb「決まる」(be officially decided) or the transitive verb「決める」(make a decision or resolve). Only「～に決まっている」is the grammar pattern expressing a subjective, inevitable judgment. Example:「こんなに練習したんだから、合格するに決まっている。」(I’ve practiced this much, so I’m sure I’ll pass.)

The sentence means: “Don’t stay cooped up at home all day—let’s go see a movie!” A similar example is:「せっかくの休日だから、みんなでパーッと飲みに行こうじゃないか。」(Since it’s a rare day off, let’s all go out for a good drink!) In an exam, when you see a verb in the volitional form, such as 行こう, prioritize「〜じゃないか」as an invitation pattern. Do not confuse it with「〜ようともしない」, which negatively describes a third person making no attempt to do something.

default.q.test-35-q2-2.why.1: ✗ (b) 「〜（よう）ともしない」 describes someone having absolutely no intention of doing something, so it is not used for invitations or suggestions.
default.q.test-35-q2-2.why.2: ✓ (c) 「〜ようじゃないか」 is an N2 grammar pattern that follows the volitional form to express a suggestion or invitation to do something together.
default.q.test-35-q2-2.why.3: ✗ (d) 「〜ともする」 does not form a suitable grammar structure for making a suggestion when combined with the volitional form of a verb.
default.q.test-35-q20-20.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) 入らないこともない

It gives a cautious or hesitant affirmation: “it is not impossible; it can be done if there is sufficient effort or the right condition.” In the dialogue, the complete translation is: “This concert is very popular, and I hear all the tickets have sold out. I wonder if there is any way to get one. / It’s not that we can’t get one, but would it be all right if it costs a little more?” Compare:「毎日練習すれば、弾けないこともありません。」(If you practice every day, it is not that you cannot play it.) Do not confuse it with 「〜はずはない」in (b), which makes an absolute claim based on logical reasoning. The expression in the question has the tentative, concessive nuance reinforced by the conjunction「けど」.
default.q.test-35-q20-20.why.0: ✗ (a) Repeating the verb as 「入るとすれば入る」 does not form a natural Japanese sentence pattern and does not express conditional feasibility.
default.q.test-35-q20-20.why.1: ✗ (b) The structure 「〜はずはない」 expresses an absolutely certain judgment based on logic, which is too assertive and conflicts with the context of the tickets being sold out and the hesitation in the following clause.
default.q.test-35-q20-20.why.2: ✗ (c) The phrase 「入るなら入る」 is not a commonly used grammar pattern and does not express the idea of managing to find a way to obtain a ticket.
default.q.test-35-q20-20.why.3: ✓ (d) The pattern「〜ないこともない」expresses a double negative (“it is not that it is impossible”), which fits the context perfectly: getting a ticket is possible, but only by accepting a higher price.

The pattern「〜はともかく（として）」sets aside the subject in the first clause (children with weak physical strength) to emphasize the surprising and unbelievable point in the second clause (even adults died).
default.q.test-35-q21-21.explanation: The structure 「N + はともかく（として）」 means “setting X aside for the moment” and is used when the speaker wants to emphasize that the following point Y is much more important or surprising than the obvious point X. The complete sentence can be translated as: “Setting aside the fact that young children have weak resistance, no one could have imagined that even adults would die from such a disease.” Another example is: 「値段はともかくとして、デザインがとても気に入った。」(Setting aside whether it is expensive or cheap, I really like the design.) To avoid confusing it with 「〜はもちろん〜も」 (affirming that both A and B share the same quality), remember that 「〜はともかく」 deliberately sets A aside to highlight the unusual or unbelievable nature of B.
default.q.test-35-q21-21.why.0: ✗ (a) 「もちろん」 is an adverb meaning “of course” and cannot directly follow the particle 「は」 to form a contrasting clause in this context.

default.q.test-35-q21-21.why.2: ✗ (c) 「〜ぬきで」 means “excluding” or “without something” (such as leaving out onions or skipping greetings), so it does not fit the logic or meaning of the sentence.
default.q.test-35-q21-21.why.3: ✗ (d) 「〜反面」 describes two opposing aspects of the same matter; it is not used to compare the degree of two objects.

✅ Correct answer: (d) 認めるべきだ
The pattern 「〜べきだ」 combines with the dictionary form of a verb to express the speaker’s judgment that something should be done as a matter of common sense. It fits the request for the dormitory to allow the lights to remain on longer during exams.
default.q.test-35-q22-22.explanation: The structure 「V-る + べきだ」 (for 「する」, both 「すべき」 and 「するべき」 are possible) expresses the speaker's subjective judgment that something should or must be done according to common sense, conscience, or moral principles. The complete sentence means: "The dormitory rules say that the lights must be turned off at midnight, but I think the hours should be extended during exam periods; however, in reality, things are not that simple." For comparison: 「約束したことは最後まで守るべきだ。」(Promises should be kept to the very end.) To avoid confusion with the other options, remember that 「〜てならない」 and 「〜ないではいられない」 are used only for spontaneous, uncontrollable emotions or psychological impulses, not for proposing a reasonable solution as 「〜べきだ」 does.
default.q.test-35-q22-22.why.0: ✗ (a) 「〜てならない」 expresses an overwhelming, uncontrollable emotion or feeling (“extremely...”); it is not used for a rule or proposal such as 認める.
default.q.test-35-q22-22.why.1: ✗ (b) 「〜ようがない」 means that there is absolutely no way or method to do something; it does not fit a context in which an opinion or proposal is being offered.
default.q.test-35-q22-22.why.2: ✗ (c) 「〜ないではいられない」 expresses being unable to restrain oneself and being compelled to do something; it is not used to make a proposal directed at someone else.
default.q.test-35-q22-22.why.3: ✓ (d) 「〜べきだ」combines with the dictionary form of a verb to express an opinion or a moral obligation about what one should do. It combines naturally with 「〜と思う」to state a personal view.
default.q.test-35-q23-23.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) だけに
The grammar pattern 「〜だけに」means “precisely because…,” explaining that because the mother is elderly, the concern about her slow recovery is even greater.
default.q.test-35-q23-23.explanation: The pattern 「〜だけに」 combines with the plain form of a verb or adjective, and a na-adjective may retain な. It means “precisely because... even more / naturally...” and emphasizes that a particular premise causes the emotion, evaluation, or result in the following clause to be stronger than usual. The complete sentence means: “My mother fell and broke a bone while she was out shopping; precisely because she is elderly, I am even more worried that her recovery will be slow.” Compare it with: 「一生懸命練習しただけに、試合に負けたときの悔しさは大きかった。」 (“Precisely because I had practiced so hard, the disappointment of losing the match was even greater.”). Learners often confuse this pattern with option (a), 「〜ほどに」. Remember that 「ほどに」 simply describes a corresponding degree or comparative limit, whereas 「だけに」 takes a specific cause in the preceding clause and explains a corresponding subjective emotion or expectation, such as 心配だ, 嬉しい, or さすがだ.
default.q.test-35-q23-23.why.0: ✗ (a) 「〜ほどに」indicates degree (“to the extent that...”) or a proportional relationship (“the more... the more...”); it is not used to state the cause of anxiety in the following clause.
default.q.test-35-q23-23.why.1: ✗ (b) 「〜かと思うと」 describes an unexpected action occurring immediately after another action has just ended; it is completely wrong in meaning and sentence logic here.
default.q.test-35-q23-23.why.2: ✗ (c) 「〜くらい」 is used to estimate or compare degree (“to the extent of / about”), and does not function as a conjunction indicating the reason for an anxious feeling.
default.q.test-35-q23-23.why.3: ✓ (d) 「〜だけに」means “precisely because..., all the more...” or “naturally...” It appropriately connects advanced age with an unusually high level of concern.
default.q.test-35-q24-24.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) すぎない
The pattern ～にすぎない expresses the meaning “only” or “nothing more than,” which perfectly fits the context of downplaying the rumor in the following sentence.
default.q.test-35-q24-24.explanation: The structure 「N / V (plain form) + にすぎない」 means “only...; nothing more than...,” emphasizing that something is less significant, simpler, or less serious than people may think. The full sentence means: “Some people may say various bad things about him, but that is nothing more than groundless gossip; I do not care about it at all.” To solve this type of question, focus on 「少しも気にしてない」(not care in the slightest) in the second clause. This is the key clue that the speaker dismisses the rumor, making 〜にちがいない (strong supposition) easy to eliminate. Contrastive example: 私は自分ができることをやったにすぎない。(I only did what I could.)
default.q.test-35-q24-24.why.0: ✗ (a) 〜にちがいない expresses a strong inference (“must be; surely”), which does not match the dismissive attitude in the following sentence.
default.q.test-35-q24-24.why.1: ✗ (b) 〜にかぎらない means “not limited to...” or “not only...,” so it does not fit the semantic logic of the sentence.
default.q.test-35-q24-24.why.2: ✓ (c) 〜にすぎない means “only...” or “nothing more than...,” downplaying the degree and emphasizing that it is merely an unimportant rumor.
default.q.test-35-q24-24.why.3: ✗ (d) 〜におよばない means “there is no need to do something” or “does not compare with,” so it is completely inappropriate in this context.
default.q.test-35-q25-25.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) どころではなかった
The grammar 「〜どころではなかった」 is the best fit because it expresses being so overwhelmed with schoolwork and exhausted that there was no time or mental energy to go out.
default.q.test-35-q25-25.explanation: The pattern 「V-る / N + どころではない」, changing to どころではなかった in the past, means “this is no time for…” or “I am in no condition to…”. It is used when a serious or more pressing situation takes up all of the speaker’s attention and prevents another activity. In the exam context, 「勉強に追われ遊びに行くどころではなかった。夜もほとんど眠っていなかったのだから」means: “I was so overwhelmed with studying that I was in no condition to go out; I could hardly sleep at night either.” For comparison: 「熱が高くて、勉強どころではない。」 (I have such a high fever that I can’t possibly study.) Do not confuse it with (c) 「べきではなかった」, which expresses regret or criticism about an action that was already taken. Here, the speaker was prevented from going out by a lack of time and difficult circumstances and never went out.
default.q.test-35-q25-25.why.0: ✗ (a) The phrase 「ひまがあった」, meaning “had free time,” is completely opposite in meaning to the busy study schedule and lack of sleep described in the two clauses.
default.q.test-35-q25-25.why.1: ✗ (b) The pattern 「〜にほかならない」(is precisely / is nothing other than) is used to assert the sole reason for something. It does not express whether an action can or cannot be carried out.
default.q.test-35-q25-25.why.2: ✗ (c) The sentence ending 「〜べきではなかった」 (“should not have”) expresses regret or blame for something that was done, whereas the context says that the character had no opportunity or ability to go out.
default.q.test-35-q25-25.why.3: ✓ (d) The structure 「〜どころではなかった」 means “there was no time or state of mind for...” and accurately expresses that the circumstances were so busy that going out was impossible.
default.q.test-35-q3-3.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) ならない
The pattern 「〜てならない」 expresses an intense, spontaneous emotion or desire that cannot be restrained, correctly combining with the desire form 「会いたくて」.
default.q.test-35-q3-3.explanation: The grammar pattern 「〜てならない」 (V-て / A-くて / na-で + ならない) expresses emotions, mental states, or physical sensations that arise naturally within the speaker with overwhelming intensity and cannot be restrained. The complete sentence 「もう３年も国に帰っていないので、両親に会いたくてならない。」 means: “I have not returned to my country for three years, so I desperately want to see my parents.” For example: 「合格できるかどうか、結果が出るまで心配でならない。」 (I am terribly worried about whether I will pass until the results are released.) As a quick test-taking tip, the other choices—「きれない」, 「ほかない」, and 「しかない」—never combine directly after the 「〜て」 form. Therefore, when an emotion or desire appears in the 「〜て」 form, such as 「会いたくて」, the correct answer must be an expression of extreme emotion: 「〜てならない / 〜てたまらない / 〜てしょうがない」.
default.q.test-35-q3-3.why.0: ✗ (a) 「〜きれない」 combines with the ます-stem of a verb and means “cannot finish doing” or “cannot do completely”; it does not combine with the 「〜て」 form.
default.q.test-35-q3-3.why.1: ✗ (b) 「〜ほかない」 combines with the dictionary form of a verb and means “have no choice but to do something,” so it is grammatically incorrect after 「〜て」.
default.q.test-35-q3-3.why.2: ✗ (c) 「〜しかない」 combines only with a verb in the dictionary form to mean “there is no other choice”; it cannot be combined with the 「〜て」 form.
default.q.test-35-q3-3.why.3: ✓ (d) 「〜てならない」combines correctly with an い-adjective in the「〜くて」form to express an intense desire, such as “want very much to meet...”.

✅ Correct answer: (a) ものか
The pattern「V-る + ものか」combined with「２度と」expresses strong denial and an absolute determination never to repeat the action.
default.q.test-35-q4-4.explanation: The pattern 「V-る / A-い / A-な / N+な + ものか」(colloquially: もんか) expresses emphatic, absolute negation, with the force of “I certainly won’t…” or “As if I would…”. In this sentence, it combines with the adverb 「２度と」 to mean: “I’ll never set foot in such an expensive restaurant again!” Compare: 「あんなやつに負けるものか。」(As if I would lose to someone like him!) To distinguish 「ものか」 from 「ことか」, remember that 「ものか」 is a firm rejection or negation, whereas 「ことか」 is used with degree expressions such as 「どんなに / どれほど」 to express deep exclamation.
default.q.test-35-q4-4.why.0: ✓ (a) 「〜ものか」follows a verb in dictionary form and, together with 「２度と」, expresses strong negation and a firm determination never to do that again.
default.q.test-35-q4-4.why.1: ✗ (b) 「〜ことか」is an exclamatory pattern meaning “how...” or “what a...,” often used with 「どんなに／どれほど」, and does not mean negating an action.
default.q.test-35-q4-4.why.2: ✗ (c) 「〜ようだ」 expresses an inference based on impressions or comparison (“seems” or “appears”), not the speaker’s subjective volition or determination.
default.q.test-35-q4-4.why.3: ✗ (d) 「〜だろう」expresses an approximate conjecture (“probably / I suppose”), so it is not suitable for expressing negative determination together with 「２度と」.
default.q.test-35-q5-5.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 分からなくなった
The adverb 「かえって」indicates a result completely contrary to the original intention: the speaker asked their older brother for an explanation to understand the lesson, but ended up understanding it even less.
default.q.test-35-q5-5.explanation: The N2 adverb 「かえって」 (“on the contrary” or “instead”) often combines with conditional forms such as 「～たら／ば／と」 to describe a situation in which an action is performed with good intentions, but the actual result is completely contrary to the initial expectation, usually with an unfavorable outcome. The complete sentence means, “I couldn’t do my math homework by myself, and when I asked my older brother to explain it, I understood even less instead.” A typical example is 「良かれと思ってアドバイスしたのに、かえって相手を怒らせてしまった。」 (“I gave advice with good intentions, but instead I made the other person even angrier.”). Do not choose (a) 「分かってきた」 merely because the sentence mentions having an explanation. Remember that 「かえって」 must lead to an opposite or disappointing result compared with the original purpose.
default.q.test-35-q5-5.why.0: ✗ (a) This expresses a result that follows the initial expectation, directly conflicting with the meaning of 「かえって」, which indicates the opposite result.
default.q.test-35-q5-5.why.1: ✗ (b) This is an intentional subsequent action, not an unexpected resulting state arising contrary to expectations from the older brother’s teaching.
default.q.test-35-q5-5.why.2: ✓ (c) This correctly expresses a negative result that goes against the original purpose and combines properly with 「かえって」.
default.q.test-35-q5-5.why.3: ✗ (d) Incorrect because it does not form a logically meaningful sentence or express an unexpected result contrary to expectations in this context.
default.q.test-35-q6-6.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) うまいとは言えない
The grammar pattern 「～割には」 describes a result that is contrary to or disproportionate to the expectation established in the preceding clause. Thus, “the restaurant is expensive, but one cannot say that it is delicious” is the most appropriate choice.
default.q.test-35-q6-6.explanation: The pattern 「～割には」follows the plain form of a verb or i-adjective, retains 「な」after a na-adjective, and takes 「の」after a noun. It indicates that the result in the following clause does not match, or contrasts with, the standard or expectation suggested in the preceding clause. The complete sentence means “Although this restaurant is expensive, it can hardly be called delicious.” Compare: 「彼は年の割には若く見える。」(He looks young for his age.) Unlike expressions such as 「～て当然」(as expected), the clause following 「～割には」must contain a contrast or unexpected result.
default.q.test-35-q6-6.why.0: ✓ (a) It is semantically appropriate because 「～割には」 expresses the contrast between the high price and the food not being as delicious as expected.
default.q.test-35-q6-6.why.1: ✗ (b) 「うまくて当然だ」(it is only natural that it tastes good) describes an expected result, contradicting the unexpected or contrary result expressed by 「～割には」.
default.q.test-35-q6-6.why.2: ✗ (c) It is incorrect because 「うまくてしようがない」 means “it is so delicious that it is unbearable,” expressing an extremely positive feeling that does not fit the mismatched evaluative nuance of the structure.
default.q.test-35-q6-6.why.3: ✗ (d) うまいと思う (“I think it is tasty”) merely expresses ordinary subjective agreement; it does not create a paradoxical contrast with the high price.
default.q.test-35-q7-7.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) 見てもつまらない
The preceding clause states that the film is intended for adults (大人向け). Combined with the concessive structure 「〜ても」, the logical result is that children would find it boring even if they watched it.
default.q.test-35-q7-7.explanation: The suffix 「〜向け」(N + 向け) means designed, produced, or intended for a particular group N. Combined with the concessive form 「〜ても」(V-ても: even if...), it can describe a natural or unfavorable result. The complete sentence means: "This movie was made for adults, so even if children watch it, they will probably find it boring." Example: 「この本は専門家向けだから、初心者が読んでも理解できない。」(This book is intended for specialists, so even beginners who read it cannot understand it.) Do not confuse this with 「〜ところだ」, which describes the timing of an action—about to do, currently doing, or having just done something—not an evaluation or impression of an object or work.
default.q.test-35-q7-7.why.0: ✗ (a) 「見てもおもしろい」 (“it is still interesting even when watched”) logically contradicts the preceding reason that the film is intended exclusively for adults.
default.q.test-35-q7-7.why.1: ✓ (b) This is correct because the context indicates that the film is aimed at adults, so it is entirely reasonable that children would find it boring even if they watched it (見てもつまらない).
default.q.test-35-q7-7.why.2: ✗ (c) This is incorrect because 「V-るところだ」describes an action that is about to take place, so it is semantically unsuitable when combined with the cause in the first clause.
default.q.test-35-q7-7.why.3: ✗ (d) 「〜ところではない」 means “this is not the time for...” or “not in the state of mind to...,” so it is completely unrelated to evaluating the impression expressed in the sentence.

✅ Correct answer: (c) 無理だった
The pattern 「〜ものの」 expresses a contrast in which the actual result does not meet expectations after an attempt. Therefore, 「無理だった」 (it was too difficult; it could not be done) is the only correct choice.

The complete sentence means: "I heard that the game was very popular with young people, so I tried playing it too, but it was really too much for me." The phrase 「わたしには〜」often appears with evaluations of ability or feasibility, such as 無理だ or 難しい. The clause after 「〜ものの」therefore has an unfavorable nuance, allowing us to eliminate the positive statement in (a) and the contextually illogical choices (b) and (d).

default.q.test-35-q8-8.why.1: ✗ (b) Given the context of a game aimed at young people, the speaker cannot describe themself as “too young” (若すぎた).
default.q.test-35-q8-8.why.2: ✓ (c) Correct because 「無理だった」 (“was too much” / “could not be managed”) fully expresses the unfavorable result, contrary to expectations after trying the game.
default.q.test-35-q8-8.why.3: ✗ (d) This is incorrect because 「年を取っていた」 does not combine naturally with 「わたしには〜」, which evaluates ability and suitability.
default.q.test-35-q9-9.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) 開かないわけだ
The pattern 〜わけだ expresses a realization—“No wonder...” or “That explains why...” after discovering the cause, in this case using the wrong key.
default.q.test-35-q9-9.explanation: The structure 「plain form (普) + わけだ」 expresses realization of the obvious reason for something after the speaker has learned its cause, with the sense of “no wonder...” or “so that’s why...” The complete sentence means, “I tried my hardest to open the door, but it wouldn’t open. After checking the key again, I finally realized: no wonder the door wouldn’t open—I had the wrong key.” A similar example is 「東京は物価が高いわけだ、家賃がこんなに高いなんて知らなかった。」 (“No wonder prices are so high in Tokyo; I had no idea rent was this expensive.”). To distinguish it from the cause structure (b) 「〜せいだ」, remember that 「〜せいだ」 comes directly after the cause, such as having the wrong key, whereas 「〜わけだ」 follows the obvious result, such as the door not opening, and expresses the realization that comes after learning the cause.
default.q.test-35-q9-9.why.0: ✗ (a) Incorrect because it means “no wonder it can be opened,” which directly contradicts the actual situation that the door cannot be opened (開かない).
default.q.test-35-q9-9.why.1: ✗ (b) This is incorrect because 〜せいだ expresses a cause leading to a negative result; in this position, it reverses the causal order between using the wrong key and the door not opening.
default.q.test-35-q9-9.why.2: ✗ (c) 〜ことだ is used to give advice or an instruction (“you should / need to do something”), so it does not fit this context.
default.q.test-35-q9-9.why.3: ✓ (d) Correct because 〜わけだ with a negative form clearly expresses understanding of the reason: “No wonder the door would not open,” after realizing that the wrong key was being held.
default.q.test-36-q1-1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) ことだ
The structure 「V-る／V-ない + ことだ」 is used to give advice or suggest that someone should or should not do something in a specific situation.
default.q.test-36-q1-1.explanation: The pattern 「V-る / V-ない + ことだ」 means "should / should not do something" and is used to give direct, practical advice or the best solution for a specific situation. The complete sentence means: "If you are so dissatisfied with what other people do, you should try doing it yourself; only then will you understand how hard it is for them." Another example is: 「日本語が上手になりたいなら、毎日少しでも話すことだ。」 (If you want to improve your Japanese, you should speak a little every day.) Remember that 「ことだ」 gives personal advice about a specific situation. Do not confuse it with 「はずだ」 (should be; logical expectation) or 「ものだ」 (advice based on general social norms or common wisdom).

default.q.test-38-q1-1.why.3: ✓ (d) 「〜というわけだ」expresses a natural and reasonable conclusion, clarifying that the parents’ thinking changed precisely because of the preceding reality.

default.q.test-38-q16-16.verdict:

The complete sentence means: “Recently, many young people quit immediately after finding a job; no wonder the Japanese-style belief that one should work for life at a single company is gradually fading.” For comparison: 医療技術が進歩しつつあるわけだから、平均寿命が延びるのも当然だ。 (Since medical technology is steadily advancing, it is only natural that average life expectancy is increasing.) When the first clause presents a concrete phenomenon and the second explains it with a meaning such as “that explains why,” choose 「〜わけだ」. Do not confuse it with 「〜ものだ」, used for general principles, or 「〜ことだ」, used for advice.

The grammar ～にすぎない comes from the negative form of 過ぎる (“to exceed”) and states that something is limited to that level, no more and no less.

Remember that it comes from the verb「過ぎる」(to exceed): 「～に過ぎない」literally means “does not exceed that level,” helping distinguish it from options related to frequency or requests.

The grammar pattern ～だらけ describes a state in which many of something cover an area, usually with a negative or unpleasant nuance.
default.q.test-6-q18-18.explanation: The structure 「N + だらけ」means “full of” or “covered with,” and directly follows a noun to describe a place or surface filled or covered with something, usually with a negative or undesirable nuance. It commonly appears with troublesome or dirty things such as 間違い (mistakes), ゴミ (trash), 泥 (mud), and 借金 (debt). Example: 「テストを返してもらったが、間違いだらけでがっかりした。」(I got my test back, but it was full of mistakes, so I was disappointed.) Remember that 「～だらけ」can be used for both physical objects and abstract concepts. Unlike 「～まみれ」, which describes something stuck to a surface, such as sweat, mud, or blood, it is not limited to physical dirt. Unlike 「～ずくめ」, it does not normally describe positive or fortunate situations.

The pattern ～なんか is the colloquial form of など. It is used to give a representative example or make a gentle suggestion in casual conversation.
default.q.test-6-q19-19.explanation: The structure 「Noun / [V-る・V-た + の] + なんか」 is the casual spoken form of the listing particle 「など」. In everyday conversation, it is often used to give an example or suggest an action or thing without being forceful. With this function, it can be translated as “for example” or “something like...” For example: 「疲れたときは、温かいお風呂に入るのなんかいいですよ。」 (When you’re tired, taking a warm bath or something like that is a good idea.) In addition to listing examples, 「なんか」 can convey belittling or dismissive nuance, or modesty when referring to oneself. It does not express ability in the negative, as in choice (a), or cause and determination, as in choice (d).
default.q.test-6-q19-19.why.0: ✗ (a) The meaning “difficult to...” or “cannot...” corresponds to structures expressing difficulty or impossibility, such as ～がたい or ～かねる.

The grammar 「～ついでに」 describes taking the opportunity, while carrying out a main action, to do an additional minor action.
default.q.test-6-q2-2.explanation: The grammar pattern 「ついでに」connects with a dictionary-form verb, past-form verb, or possessive noun (V-る / V-た / Nの + ついでに). It is used when the speaker takes advantage of an opportunity created by a planned main action to complete an additional task. Its overall meaning is “while you are at it,” “incidentally,” or “taking the opportunity to.” For example: 「買い物のついでに、図書館に寄って本を返してきた。」(While I was shopping, I stopped by the library to return some books.) To distinguish it from 「～につれて」(as...; along with...), remember that the action following 「ついでに」is always intentional and makes use of the circumstances; it is not a natural change that occurs alongside something else.

This grammar pattern expresses admiration or high praise when the actual result fully matches someone’s position, reputation, or effort.
default.q.test-6-q20-20.explanation: The patterns「～だけあって／だけのことはある」combine with the plain form (普通形) of a verb, adjective, or noun. A na-adjective retains な, while a noun may connect directly or with である. The meaning is “just as expected,” “no wonder,” or “living up to its reputation.” The pattern conveys strong praise and is used when a good result or excellent quality is naturally consistent with someone’s effort or reputation. For example: この店はミシュランの星を獲得しただけあって、どの料理も本当に素晴らしい。(No wonder this restaurant is excellent, having earned a Michelin star; every dish is truly wonderful.) Distinguish it from「～だけに」(precisely because..., all the more...), which can be used with negative results or regret, whereas「～だけあって」is used with positive results and high praise.

The structure 「V-る + ことなく」 is a formal equivalent of 「〜しないで」. It describes an action or state continuing without doing something or without something occurring.
default.q.test-6-q21-21.explanation: The pattern 「V-る + ことなく」 is a formal written equivalent of 「〜しないで」 or 「〜ずに」. It describes an action or state continuing smoothly and without interruption, without carrying out the preceding action V. This pattern directly follows a dictionary-form verb (辞書形) and often appears in speeches, formal writing, or descriptions of perseverance and sustained effort. For example, in 「彼らは休むことなく、10時間も歩き続けた」 (They continued walking for ten hours without resting), the speaker emphasizes that the walking continued without any intervening rest. To distinguish it from similar patterns containing 「こと」, such as 「〜ことから」 (indicating a cause or basis: because...) and 「〜ことなしに」 (indicating a necessary condition: without A, B cannot be done), remember that 「なく」 is the connective form of the negative 「ない」: doing the later action without doing the earlier one.

The grammar pattern ～まい expresses the speaker’s strong negative determination (“I will definitely not do it”) or a negative conjecture (“it probably will not happen”).
default.q.test-6-q22-22.explanation: The grammar pattern 「～まい」 is a formal, written-style expression used either to indicate strong negative volition ("I will never..." or "I am determined not to...") or negative conjecture ("probably not"). With a first-person subject, it combines with the dictionary form of group 1 verbs. Group 2 and group 3 verbs use either the dictionary form or the form without る, followed by まい; in particular, する becomes すまい/するまい and くる becomes こまい/くるまい. In expressions of determination, 「～まい」 often combines with adverbs such as 「二度と」 (never again) or 「決して」 (absolutely never). Example: 「あんなつらい経験は、二度とするまい。」 (I will never go through such a painful experience again.) Remember that 「まい」 is equivalent to 「～ないでおこう / ～絶対に～ない」 and is the opposite of the affirmative volitional form 「～よう」.

The pattern 「～ということだ／～とのことだ」 is commonly used in Japanese to report information received from another source or to summarize and explain the nature of a situation.
default.q.test-6-q23-23.explanation: The pattern 「Plain form + ということだ／とのことだ」has two main uses: objectively and politely relaying information that one has heard (「～とのことだ」is more formal and often appears in letters and announcements), or summarizing or inferring something in order to explain the nature of what was just mentioned. Depending on the context, it can be translated as “I hear that...” (reported information) or “that is to say / it means that...” (explanation). Example: 「天気予報によると、明日は午後から激しい雨になるということだ。」(“According to the weather forecast, there will be heavy rain from tomorrow afternoon.”) To distinguish the two meanings quickly in an exam, look at the linking expressions: if 「～によると／～では」(according to a source...) appears, it indicates reported information; if 「つまり」「要するに」(in other words, to sum up...) appears before it, it indicates an explanation.

The N2 grammar pattern 「～をめぐって」 follows a noun to indicate the topic or issue around which people argue, discuss, or hold opposing opinions.
default.q.test-6-q24-24.explanation: The structure 「N + をめぐって」 (or 「N + をめぐる + N」) derives from the verb 巡る (to go around / revolve around). It is used when an issue or matter (N) becomes the focus of opposing opinions, disputes, or discussions among multiple parties. The following clause must generally contain a verb expressing disagreement, discussion, or conflict, such as 議論する (to debate), 対立する (to be opposed), or 争う (to dispute). The complete sentence 「遺産をめぐって、兄弟の間で激しい争いが起きた」 means: "A fierce dispute broke out among the siblings over the inheritance." Another example is 「新空港の建設をめぐって、住民の間で議論が続いている」 (Discussions among residents over the construction of the new airport are continuing.) Unlike 「～に関して / ～について」, this pattern involves multiple parties whose views clash; it is not used for one person's research or presentation.

In the sentence, it fully conveys the meaning “for …” or “intended for ….” Be careful to distinguish it from 「～向き」(naturally suitable for), while 「～向け」emphasizes the creator’s original intention and purpose. Example: 「このアニメは子ども向けに作られたが、大人にも大人気だ。」 (This anime was made for children, but it is also very popular with adults.)

Verbs ending in する change to「される」in the passive (or it may be the shortened passive-causative form「V(あ)される」for some group 1 verbs). It describes an action received by the subject from another party, with either an objective or adversative nuance. The form means “be done to” or “be made,” showing that the subject receives the action. Example: 「会議で新しいプロジェクトのリーダーに彼が推薦された。」(“At the meeting, he was recommended as the leader of the new project.”). Remember that「Vされる」is an affirmative passive form; it contains no negative marker such as「ない」or「ず」.

default.q.test-6-q6-6.explanation: ～くらい／～ぐらい follows the plain form of a verb or adjective (a na-adjective retains な), or a noun. It can express degree (“to the extent that ...”), give a minimal or dismissive example (“at least”), or estimate quantity (“about, approximately”). The basic idea is to use a concrete image or event as a reference point so the listener can visualize the intensity of a state. Example:「昨日は涙が出るくらいうれしかった」(Yesterday I was so happy that I nearly cried.) Remember that this pattern is connected to measuring or estimating degree, so it should not be confused with ～しかない (“have no choice but to,” choice a) or ～を問わず (“regardless of,” choice b).

The grammar ～げ attaches to an adjective stem or verb to express the appearance, demeanor, or emotional state observed from the outside.
default.q.test-6-q7-7.explanation: The suffix ～げ attaches directly to -i adjectives (with い removed), na-adjectives (with な removed), and ます-stem verbs (with ます removed). It functions grammatically like a na-adjective, as in ～げな N and ～げに V, and also has special forms such as よさげ and なさげ. The pattern means “looking...” and expresses the speaker’s visual judgment or impression of another person’s inner state based on their facial expression or outward behavior. For example: 彼は何か言いたげな顔をしてこちらを見ていた (He looked at me with an expression that seemed to say he wanted to say something). Note that ～げ is more literary and tends to be used with words describing emotions or moods, whereas ～そう is more flexible and common in everyday conversation.

This is a characteristic grammar pattern for expressing an intense emotion, desire, or physical sensation that wells up so strongly that the speaker cannot suppress or endure it.
default.q.test-9-q25-25.explanation: Grammatically, this pattern combines with a verb te-form, an i-adjective with い changed to くて, or a na-adjective with で. It is used when the speaker experiences an intense physical sensation or psychological state. It means “extremely…,” “so … that it is unbearable,” or “cannot stand …,” expressing an emotion or sensation that the subject—usually the first person—cannot control. For example: 「一人で海外に暮らしているので、家族に会いたくてたまらない。」 (Because I live abroad alone, I miss my family terribly.) To distinguish it from similar patterns, remember that 「～てたまらない」 comes from the idea of enduring or bearing something and is often used for physical sensations such as pain or itching, or for an overwhelming desire to do something. By contrast, 「～てならない」 expresses feelings that arise spontaneously from within, such as 「心配でならない」 (cannot help worrying) or 「思えてならない」 (cannot help feeling/thinking).

default.q.test-9-q25-25.why.2: ✓ (c) Both ～てたまらない and ～てならない express an extreme degree of emotion or sensation, meaning “extremely,” “very,” or “unbearably.”

The grammar pattern 「～にかかわる」expresses that something is deeply related to, decisive for, or directly affects an important matter.
default.q.test-9-q3-3.explanation: The patterns 「N + にかかわる + N」and 「N + にかかわり／にかかわって + V」describe something that has a profound, decisive, or serious impact on the stated object. They can be translated as “affecting...” or “being closely and significantly related to....” For example: これは学校の名誉にかかわる重大な問題だ。(This is a serious issue affecting the school’s honor.) Unlike 「～に関する」, which simply introduces a topic (“about” or “related to”), 「～にかかわる」is used with nouns involving life, serious consequences, or core values, such as 命 (life), 信用 (trust), and 名誉 (honor).

The pattern ～ても is a concessive conditional. It indicates that even if the condition in the first clause occurs, the second clause still continues or produces a result contrary to what would normally be expected.
default.q.test-9-q4-4.explanation: Structurally, this pattern combines with the verb te-form (Vても), changes i-adjectives to くても, and uses でも with na-adjectives and nouns to establish a concessive hypothetical premise. It emphasizes that even when the action or state in the first clause is fulfilled, the event in the second clause proceeds normally without being affected (meaning: “Even if...”). Example: 「いくら安くても、必要のないものは買いません。」 (No matter how cheap something is, I will not buy things I do not need.) To avoid confusing it with conditional patterns such as ～たら or ～ば (“if...then”), remember that the particle 「も」 means “even/even if” and creates a contrast between the two clauses despite an obstacle.

The structure 「～たばかり」 follows a past-tense verb and indicates that an action or event has just occurred, according to the speaker’s subjective perception.
default.q.test-9-q5-5.explanation: The structure 「Vた ＋ ばかり」combines with the past form (た-form) and means “have just...,” describing an action or event that was completed recently. The key point is that “recently” depends on the speaker’s subjective perception. Therefore, an event that occurred several weeks or months ago may still be described with this pattern if it feels recent to the speaker. For example: 「この靴は先週買ったばかりなのに、もう汚れてしまった。」 (Even though I only bought these shoes last week, they have already gotten dirty.) Distinguish it from 「～たところ」: 「～たところ」refers to an action that has just ended according to an objective time frame of seconds or minutes, while 「～たばかり」is more flexible and depends on the speaker’s perception.

The structure 「〜ところをみると」 indicates that the speaker uses an observed fact or phenomenon as a basis for making a judgment or inference.
default.q.test-9-q8-8.explanation: 「〜ところをみると」usually combines with the plain form of a verb, most commonly V-た or V-ている, and means "judging from/based on the fact that..." The speaker directly observes an objective sign or phenomenon and uses it as evidence for an inference, so the following clause typically contains a subjective inference such as 「〜だろう」, 「〜ようだ」, or 「〜に違いない」. For comparison: 「電気が消えているところをみると、彼はもう寝たようだ」(Judging from the fact that the light is off, he seems to have gone to bed already.) To avoid confusion, 「〜からみると」indicates an evaluative viewpoint or standpoint, while 「〜向け」means intended for a particular group. 「〜ところをみると」must be based on a specific observable phenomenon used as evidence for an inference.

The grammar pattern ～限りでは limits the information serving as the basis for the speaker’s judgment, such as what they have heard, seen, learned, or investigated.
default.q.test-9-q9-9.explanation: The patterns 「V-る／V-た／V-ている + 限りでは」and 「N + の限りでは」are commonly used with verbs involving the collection or reception of information, such as 見る (see), 聞く (hear), 調べる (investigate), and 知る (know). The speaker uses this pattern to make a judgment or conclusion limited to the information they have personally accessed, implicitly indicating that they cannot be certain beyond that scope. It therefore means “as far as...” or “within the limits of what I know/hear/see...” Example: 「私が調べた限りでは、この地域にそのような習慣はありません。」(“As far as I have investigated, there is no such custom in this area.”) To distinguish it quickly, check whether the preceding word refers to an information-gathering or information-receiving action, so that it is not confused with the risk-related structure 「～恐れがある」or the intermediary expression 「～を通して」.

It is more formal than 「〜とき」 and is commonly used in instructions, technical procedures, and official contexts. In the passage describing how to prepare usucha, 「薄茶は茶杓1杯半を1人分として、柄杓半杯の湯を入れ茶筅で撹拌する。」 is followed by a sentence clarifying differences in whisking among schools: 「三千家ではそれぞれ、たっぷりと泡を立てるのが裏千家、うっすらと泡立てるのが表千家、もっとも泡が少ないのが武者小路千家といわれる。」 The sentence to be completed specifies when the tea is stirred. With choice (d), the complete sentence means: "When whisking with a chasen, the way the tea is whisked differs depending on the school." The key reason to reject choice (a), 「撹拌したときに」, is that the past form 「〜した」 suggests that the stirring has already finished, whereas the differences in foaming occur during the process, so the dictionary form 「撹拌する」 is required. Also distinguish this from 「〜うちに」, which describes gradual change over time, and 「〜最中」, which describes an ongoing action interrupted by an unexpected event. Therefore, 「〜際」 is the most natural and accurate answer.
